In my own district I have a lot of Galicians. And if the Minister of the Interior can send us more Galicians they will be welcome. If my hon. friend from Alberta is not satisfied with these in his district, let him send them to my district and I will be very glad. For, those we have there are doing remarkably well. I have heard it said in this House and out of it and have seen it in the press that these people were immoral and dishonest. My knowledge of the Galicians lead me to believe that there is as high a percentage of honesty among them as thete

is among any other people of tlie country or out of It. There are exceptions, of course ; but these exceptions are not enough to condemn a whole class. I attended an agricultural fair last fall at which several Galicians had exhibits. And one of those exhibits was the finest hog I ever saw outside of Toronto fair. The Galicians took as many prizes as any other class in proportion to the number of their entries. The hon. member for Alberta says they will not assimilate, and he went on to say that they would block the establishment of school districts. That may have happened in Alberta, but it has not happened in my district. The Galicians have a thirst for knowledge, and they want schools established. There are many ranchers in that country, Canadians and others, who would do more to prevent the starting of school districts than these Galicians would. Now, I have a few words to say with regard to the Doukhobors. I have employed them. I have had a Doukliolior woman in my house for the last year, and she is a first-class servant; and I have had her husband working for me, and he is a first-class man. They have a boy of six or seven years old, and he is attending the public schools under the direction of his parents, and he speaks English as well as my own boy does. I do not share the fear of my hon. friend from Alberta that these people will not assimilate. Why, when the Mennonites were settled here twenty-two or twenty-three years ago, exactly the same things were said about them. I do not see much difference between the Doukhobors and the Men-nonites so far as the objections that are raised are concerned. The Mennonites were placed on land in Manitoba that was not considered good for anything. But let hon. gentlemen opposite go to that country and see the perfect paradise that these people have made out of the district that they have settled, and I am sure they will not criticise this class of immigration as they have been doing. The older people among the Mennonites remain in Manitoba, but the young men are moving out. Hundreds of them are coming to my district. And these young people abandon the old customs of their fathers. At Kosthern we have several thousands of Mennonites, Germans and others. They have started public school districts all over. They have built two large roller mills, and they have established a town of several hundred population, and in the seven years since they started, they have exported about half a million bushels of grain. This goes to show that these people will develop and the second generation at any rate will be all right. I think that the money that has been spent by the department in the last three years has been well spent. We see the effect in the homestead entries. In the last year of the last government, the entries numbered about 1,500, and last year they have increased to nearly 7,000. There is another class of immigration that we are receiving and concerning which very little has been said-people from the United States. The hon. member for Alberta said there were about a million Canadians in the United States, and that it was desirable to get them back. So it is. And since this government came into power these people are coming back-hundreds and thousands of them-not only into the North-west, but into Quebec and other parts of the Dominion. Those who come to the North-west are first-class settlers. The knowledge of a prairie country that they have gained in the United States fits them to do well in our country. We are getting from the United States also a great many Germans and other foreigners, many of whom have been in the United States for twenty-five or thirty years but who find that their holdings are too small for their large families of boys, and they are selling out their land where they get $40 to $50 an acre, and are moving into the North-west Territories. And they do not come empty-handed. Some of them are bringing $10,000, some of them $20,000 in hard cash to be spent in the North-west, besides all their stock and other things. We are getting thousands and thousands of these people. Hon. gentlemen opposite never give the government credit for anything of that kind; they can only howl against the Galicians and the Doukhobors. In one sense they must be glad these people have come in, for otherwise, so far as the west is concerned, hon. gentlemen opposite would have no policy. And hon. gentlemen can see by the majorities given to the Liberal candidates that the people of that country take very little stock in it all. It may have had some effect here in the east, but, so far as the North-west is concerned it had no effect. In my own district the development is something wonderful. There is an Indian reserve that had never been taken up by the Indians. It was opened up for settlement three years ago. This reserve is about ten miles square, and there is a lot of good country all around it. I passed over that track three years ago, and there was nothing there-it was a wilderness. Last fall at the time of the election I had occasion to go through it again, standing on a little iiill I counted fourteen windmills on top of big bank barns. I saw houses there that were as good as any in the town in which I live. I went into one of them and found it furnished as well as a house in town. I saw ten and fifteen teams of horses working there. One man told me that he had brought in $25,000 in cash, besides his implements, horses, cattle, &c. That gentleman has a section of land under cultivation this year and next year he will have two sections. That is an example of what Is going on all over the Northwest, and what has been going on since the present minister took over the office and

adopted Uis present policy with reference to immigration. I am sorry to near lion, members, particularly those from my own section, talk about cutting down the amount of money spent on immigration. Why, the country is large enough to sustain a population of 60,000,000, and you must spend money to populate it.
Fut four or five millions of people in there : If you are getting into the public treasury something like $50,000,000 out of the five or six millions of people that we have now, you will get $80,000,000 or $90,000,000 when you have increased the population by that number. What would the $400,000 a year that we are spending on immigration amount to in comparison to that ? Every good settler you put on the soil is worth thousands of dollars to the whole people of this country. The people of the east are interested in this question as well as we are, because, as the development of that country goes on, the development of the eastern part goes on. What supports the manufacturing industries of this country ? The very people that consume the products that are manufactured, and we in the west are the greatest consumers in the whole Dominion of certain classes of products. Look [DOT] at the amount of agricultural machinery we use in that country. We manufacture nothing, we produce grain ; and I submit, with all due deference to the member for Alberta, that I do not care who it is that tears up the prairie and grows the grain, he is an accession to that country, although he may not be as cleanly as my bon. friend would have us think. With reference to the Doukho-bors, there is no more cleanly people in the world, in their dress, and in their houses, or a more thrifty people. They have not been placed on the best land in the country. In my district they have been placed on the very worst portions of the land. There was a colony placed at the elbow of the Saskatchewan river, on land that no person else would take up. Even the Mennonites, the Germans, would not take it up. They have been there for two years, and they have good crops of grain. They have the finest gardens I ever saw. When I went into Battleford last fall I saw them with wagon loads of vegetables, peddling them in the town, they even had cucumbers. That town has been in existence for twenty-two years, and I do not think we ever saw a cucumber sold there until these Doukhobors came in. They are very thrifty and ablebodied men. They get work on the railroad and I want to say for the benefit of the representatives of the labour organizations in this House, that they do not cut wages, they will not work for low wages. They go and earn money, and the women and boys and the old men stay at home and do the farm work. When the men come back with their money in the fall they invest it in cattle, in sheep, in horses, Mr. DAVIS.
horses for the purpose of breaking up the prairie and assisting in the development of the country. I say these people are getting along, and it is too bad that, for the sake of making a little cheap political capital out of this thing, it should be made a party question, and that these people should be abused as they have been abused in the party press of this country. That proclamation or manifesto that was published, and which the hon. member for Selkirk spoke about, is the work of only one crank. There are cranks amongst all classes.' I venture to think you will find cranks in the city of Montreal, and other places, who will send out manifestos in favour of the Boers. That class exist all over the world, do you wonder that there is one amongst six or seven thousand Doukhobors ? I know the Doukhobors well, I live pretty close to them, and I have seen them working, and I know they are satisfied and happy ; they are pleased with the liberty that they have here. They are good citizens, not troublesome to any person, they earn their living and pay their debts, and any people who do that are a desirable class of people. I wish to say in conclusion, that if the Minister of the Interior has any more Galicians, and the hon. member for Alberta does not wish them sent into his district, I should be happy to see the minister send them into the district of the Saskatchewan, because I think they are going to make a very good class of people. They have already commenced to marry with other classes of people, and, I understand, that is one of the objections the hon. member for Alberta has to them. There is another class of people that I will mention, that were brought in when the hon. gentlemen were in power, that is, a class of people from France brought into Duck Lake, Saskatchewan. They came in without any money, practically, and to-day, taking them from the standpoint of Ontario and Quebec, these men would be considered wealthy. There is hardly one of them who has not fifty or sixty head of cattle all paid for. their implements paid for, raising 1,000 to 3,000 bushels of grain, owing nobody in the world. They are picking up our habits and our language. They are law-abiding citizens, and I think if the minister can promote more immigration of that kind from Normandy or Brittany, it will be a good thing for the North-west Territories. I would be pleased to welcome them, or any other hard-working man, who is willing to take off his coat and go to work.

I shall not waste much time in attempting to reply to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Davis), or to the wishy-washy speech of the member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), who tried to steer to every point of the compass, but without pronouncing a definite opinion in any respect. When I was listening to the member

for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser), tlie impression created in my mind was, that tlie government liad made a mistake in not having made that hon. member the immigration commissioner in Europe. He has evidently missed his vocation in studying law. Judging from his speech to-night, he would have far surpassed those commissioners and agents who have been sent over by the Minister of the Interior to promote immigration from the countries of Europe. I have another fault to find with him. For more than 1800 years we had never heard from the Galatians. Since the time that the apostle Paul wrote his epistle to them, we had heard very little about them until to-night. But, the member for Guysborough has resurrected them. To-day we have the member for Guysborough giving the highest character to those Galatians. For 1,800 years we have been asking what had become of them, and now, to our surprise, the member for Guysborough brings the Galatians into our view, and gives them a certificate of character. The member for Guysborough also has a grand eulogy for these Galicians, that some persons call Galatians. There are no people in any country, apparently, to equal the Galicians and the Doukhobors, except himself, the hon. member for Guysborough. He has a sneer for the Englishman who comes to this country. It is true, he has a little eulogy for the Irishman and the Scotchman, but they are not to be compared with the Doukhobor and the Galician. I am told that the Galicians had not been a year in this country until the authorities in Winnipeg found it necessary to hang two of them for murder. That was not a very good recommendation to start with, but apparently that does not count for much with the member for Guysborough.
Those two men were brought in under the former Conservative government ; they were hang-dogs.

That is very clever, and the Minister of Customs is overwhelmed with laughter. Two Galicians were hung, and the only reply of the member for Selkirk is, that they were brought in by the Conservatives when they were in power. If the Conservatives made a mistake and brought in a few of them, what are we to say of this government, who, having known the character of their men, and having assisted to hang two of them, went to work and brought in 16,000 more of these very admirable Christian characters ? The great test, the only test, the member for Guysborough will recognize, is their ability to grow wheat. If they can grow wheat it does not matter whether they are Mormons, whether they turn their wives away, whether they break the laws of the land, whe-they they ever become Canadian citizens in the true sense of the word, and British subjects ; that does not matter a straw with the member for Guysborough,
so long as they can grow wheat.
It does not matter a straw to the hon. member for Guysborough if they can only grow wheat. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) has the same argument. He repeats in parrot-like fashion the statement of the hon. member for Guysborough. Let them grow wheat, let Mr. and Mrs. Doukhobor be good manservant and maidservant in my household and I shall ask for nothiug more. I agree with the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), whose able speech tonight upon this question deserves to be read and considered by every Canadian because he has laid down the true principles which should guide the government of the people in the matter of immigration into this country. Sir, it is true that me great bulk of the population of Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and latterly of the province of British Columbia, is made up of people from the eastern provinces of Canada. The nroof of it, if proof were necessary, is shown in one fact that I shall state, that in the province of Ontario this year the Minister of Education, in his report, states that there are about 7,000 less children attending the public schools in Ontario than there were in the previous year. I have a letter from the Minister of Education of the province of Quebec in which he says that there are a thousand less children attending the public schools, or what are considered to be public schools in Quebec, than there were in the former year. What has become of these children ? Their parents and themselves have gone to the North-west Territories. They have built up the country very largely, together with Englishmen, Irishmen, and Scotchman from the old land. The hon. member for Guysborough, though he has a little word of commendation for the Irishman and the Scotchman, sneers at the Englishmen. Mr. Speaker, the time has gone by when an Englishman need be put out at the sneer of the hon. member for Guysborough. The Englishman has taken his part with the Irishman and the Scotchman, in civilizing the world. That illustrious trio, not only on land but on the sea, have upheld the honour of the British flag, they have upheld the [DOT] honour of the greatest nation that the world has ever seen and they have promoted the colonization and settlement of the four quarters of the globe. You cannot go to any civilized or uncivilized part of the earth today but the Englishman, the Irishman and the Scotchman have been there engaged in the promotion of civilization, commerce and Christianity. The sneers of the hon. member for Guysborough will not be considered of very great importance when we look at the illustrious history of the Englishman in all ages and no less than in the age in which we are living to-day. Next, the hon. gentleman speaks of the Mennonltes as being an admirable example of foreigners being brought into Canada and paying their debts. He said that those men who decried and

deprecated the introduction of these men in the past will look very small to-day. In this case he has only to look at his friends around him, because they were the men, when the Conservative party were in power, who denounced and opposed the introduction of the Mennonites whom he eulogized so highly to-day. But, the hon. gentleman was, in his speech, from beginning to end, constantly harping upon the fact that the Doukhobors and Mennonites paid their debts. That was another evidence of the desirability of immigration. I would bo rather of the opinion, from his constant reference to the fact that these people paid their debts, that there were some of the more desirable class of immigrants from the British Islands who did not pay their debts and that the hon. member for Guysborough was perhaps let in a little by some of these chaps. But, however that may be, the fact that a man has to pay his debts if he is worth it is only something that characterizes Canadians as a people. We all pay our debts.
No, we do not.

Well, the hon. member who interrupted and said that we do not. is evidently speaking for himself. I am sure that he is not speaking for anybody on this side of the House and I would be sorry to think that he was speaking for any of his colleagues on that side of the House, so that we will leave him as the solitary example of the men who will not pay their debts. Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), this afternoon, when I was out, though I was listening to most of his speech, made some reference,
I am told, to the prosperity and progress made in the town and district of Yorkton, North-west Territories, and gave my name as one who had participated in that prosperity. I have quite an intimate knowledge of that. We formed a colonization company more than eighteen years ago and it is a matter of very great pride to myself, personally, that, in the last local election, that district had more than 1,000 recorded votes at the election. We sent the settlers 100 ' miles in from the railway at that period. We complied as a colonization company with every condition that the government had laid down, which I do not think another company did as well ns we did. At any rate, we brought in the right kind of settlers. We brought in settlers from old Canada as well as some from the old land.

If the hon. gentleman heard that I reflected in any way upon him or upon the company of which he has spoken, he is mistaken. ' Hansard' will show him, if he reads it to-morrow, that I merely said that the value of the land owned by that company had increased largely, owing to the fact of that immigration having gone in there. I did not refer to the Mr. WALLACE.
colonization company of which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) is president, in a disparaging manner, but simply mentioned that fact.

I am glad to hear that. But, I was proceeding to say that mat company, and I think it is a matter of very great pride to every member of the company, turned the tide of the emigration of those young men who, in former years were making their way to the United States, and directed them to our own North-west Territories. Such men -as -the Merediths and other young men who went in there and have become prosperous business men and farmers, were among those whom we induced to settle there. I do not believe that there is any portion of the North-west Territories or Manitoba that is enjoying greater prosperity than the district I allude to, with which my name has been connected and to which I have devoted a large share of attention in years gone by and in all the years since. But, I say further that when the hon. member for Selkirk says that prosperity is largely due-that is as I understood him
Partly due.

Well, partly due-to the fact that the Doukhobors are settled near there. I do not share that opinion with him. The Doukhobors are settled thirty or forty miles away from Yorkton and they are the exclusive settlers in that part. But when, people say they are going into Yorkton they take objection to these Doukhobors and say: Oh, that is where the Doukhobors live. The fact that the name of Yorkton is connected with the Doukhobors, although they are forty or fifty miles away from Yorkton, has been detrimental to the whole district. Yorkton being the terminus of the Manitoba and North-western Railway, the settlers from all these districts to the north must leave the railway at Yorkton, and as people get it into their heads that the Doukhobors are settled in Yorkton- the prosperity of that part of the country has been retarded. I do not believe that the Doukhobors are a desirable class of settlers. Those men who have been proved to so lightly regard the marriage tie that by their rules and regulations they discard their wives whenever they wish, and who in other respects are guilty of loose and improper conduct, are not the kind of people we want in Canada. I do not know that we want them to assimilate with our Canadian people, but anyway they do not assimilate. The government made a mistake in putting them into a separate community, where they have exclusive lordship over the soil in that whole section of the country. If they are a desirable class of settlers, they should be sent to mingle with the other people, so as to be taught Canadian instincts ; the value of the liberty we enjoy, and the kind of institutions we live under. The Doukhobors will not learn

these things themselves and they apparently do not want to learn them. I regret that the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is not here to-night, as I wanted to bring something to his attention. His organ, his newspaper, as I am told, the Halifax Chronicle, pronounced an opinion about these Douklio-bors which I will read for the edification of the Minister of the Interior, to show him how his colleague views these Doulchobors; if the Halifax Chronicle represents his views-

It does not represent his views.
Hon, Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Nor the views of anybody else on this side of the House.
I am told the Minister of Finance was the editor of the Halifax Chronicle.

That was a good
many years ago.
Is he the editor now ?
I have failed to hear that the Halifax Chronicle has ceased to be the organ of the government.
I may tell the hon. gentleman that the Halifax Chronicle is to-day the organ of the company combines in Nova Scotia. Some of us do not recognize it as the organ of the Liberal party.
I am glad to have that information because to my mind it is one and the same thing as the organ of the Liberal party.
Only ten times more so.

Referring to the immigration of the Doukhobors, the Halifax Chronicle says :
It is well perhaps that this matter has coma up in this way, at this time. Not much damage can yet be done. The few thousands of foreign riffraff so far brought into the Dominion can probably be swept out of the country or got rid of in some way without serious injury. But we want no more of it. Immigrants have recently landed in Halifax, and not a few of them, whom all that have seen them report as anything but a promising acquisition to any civilized land, and as a most probable good riddance to their native countries.
I was very much struck with the charming description which the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) gave of these good and amiable Christian people when they first saw the shores of Halifax, but I forgot that a man who was at Halifax at the time watching these Doukhobors has written an entirely different description from that given by the hon. member for Guysborough, who did not happen to be there at all.
It is revolting in the extreme to think of blood such as this being destined to mix with our good, clean British and French Canadian blood to its certain corruption. The early filling up of our vacant lands is a small matter a3 compared with the preservation of the wholesomeness of our population. What would be thought of the sanity of the owner of a mansion and the father of a growing family who should go into the slums and fill his vacant chambers with their denizens to the pollution of his home and the probable ejection of his unborn children? There is no necessity for reckless haste in peopling the North-west. Better let the prairies lie fallow as they have lain since the waters receded from their face than plant them with residents who will be in but not of Canada ; and whom shall we be ashamed to acknowledge as bearers of the Canadian name. Population is desirable-but not undesirable population. If the department would permit us to address it in Latin we should say to it, ' Festina lente '- which, being interpreted, means ' go slow.'
I would refer that opinion of the candid friend, the Halifax Chronicle, to the serious attention of the Minister ot the Interior, who, I hope, has an open mind upon this question, because last year be apologized for the introduction of the Galicians and the Doukhobors, and said there would be scarcely any further immigration of the Doukhobors to this country, as the supply had been exhausted. It seemed a relief to the .minister (Hon. Mr. Sifton) to be able to make that announcement to the House.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) tell me who is the present editor of the Halifax Chronicle.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I may tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) that the present editor of the Halifax Chronicle

Now, I must object to this kind of thing. One gentleman over there gets up to ask me a question and another one of them gets up to answer it for me. I object to that. I contend that that game won't work.
I merely wanted to find out if it was a certain gentleman who used to edit the Free Press at Winnipeg, a Mr. McLellan, I think.
The hon. gentleman from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) will have to go elsewhere for that information.
I thought so.
I am not concerned as to who is the editor of the Halifax Chronicle, I am only concerned in the wisdom of his remarks.
We are concerned in the west, as we know the gentleman.

I am concerned with the fact that there is one Liberal newspaper in the country that gives words of sound wisdom to its readers, because we do not always find that to be the case. Has the hon. member for Selkirk anything to say

against the editor of the Halifax Chronicle, even if he should turn out to he that gentleman from the Winnipeg Free Press ?
I say we know that gentleman, that is all. In the west he is pretty well known.

Merely knowing does not convey any idea to this House unless the sneer that accompanies the remark means that he is a disreputable character or an unreliable man. I would like to hear the hon. member, who knows all about him, tell us what his opinion is of this editor of the Halifax Chronicle.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Would the hon. gentleman allow me to say that he was not in Halifax when the Doukho-bors arrived, and he never saw any of them, and he was not at that time an editor of the Chronicle.

I would like to know where the hon. member gets his information as to the whereabouts of this individual.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I can give the hon. gentleman that information if he wants it.

Apparently every man in the Liberal party who has an independent opinion, and who is not afraid to express his independent opinion, is hooted down by the members of the Liberal party, and we have the hon. member for Selkirk and the hon. member for Victoria, N.S., both casting their sneers at this gentleman. It would be better for them to reply to his statements than to asperse the character of the man. The important matter to us is whether his statements are true and his opinions sound. In my judgment his opinions are exceedingly sound, and represent the proper and true opinion of the people of Canada. Now, the hon. member for Selkirk told us in glowing and eloquent terms what they were going to do in the future, and the great results that were going to be accomplished by this enormous expenditure on immigration, more than double the expenditure during the last years of the Conservative regime. Why did the hon. gentleman not tell us of the great results that have flowed from the policy and the acts of the government of to-day ? We were told that he was the immigration commissioner, and the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) told us that he had handled in one year $90,000 of the money of the people of Canada. Well, we would like to know where were the good results ; or had he just sown the seed and expected that the good results would follow in future years ? He was not able to point to very great improvement, although he might fairly have done so. He said there was a larger immigration into Manitoba Mr. WALLACE.
and the Territories in the last three year's than there had been in the previous three years. 1 have no doubt that is true, because Providence blessed the North-west during those three years with the most abundant crops perhaps which had ever been enjoyed there, and prices were fairly good, at any rate profitable. There was every Inducement, therefore, for the people to go up and possess the land. The railroads had opened up the country ; the people were becoming better acquainted with the resources of the country. I think myself that any man residing in any of the older provinces who is not satisfied with the conditions which obtain there, cannot do better than seek his fortune in our own North-west and British Columbia, where there is a variety of occupation, where there is mineral wealth as well as agricultural wealth, and where there are all the conditions to make a prosperous and wealthy people. So that we cannot advertise our resources in those parts of the Dominion too much, even to our own people; and we should say to them, If you are going to change your condition, if you are going to farm, farm in our own Dominion, because the conditions are more favourable there than they are in any other part of the world for increasing the prosperity and wealth of the people. The hon. member for Selkirk eulogized the Doukhobors and Galicians, followed by the hon. member for Guysborougli (Mr. Fraser), and the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), in the same strain. There was nothing too good to be done for those people, whom I for my part consider to be an undesirable element of our population. But I was reading yesterday in one of our Ottawa papers a contrast to these eulogies in the shape of the treatment which some of our own Canadian citizens received. Here is an article in the Ottawa Evening Journal of yesterday :
The Fox Bay Settlers are Leaving Manitoba- They Claim to have been Set Down in a Swamp in the Dauphin District-Sickness and Death Followed to Many, and those who Survive will Return to the East to Find a Living.
(Special to the Journal.)
Quebec, April 11.-The Fox Bay settlers are on their way back from the Dauphin district of Manitoba, where they suffered much from typhoid and then la grippe. Twelve of their number died. They were set down in a swamp and have been nearly drowned out.
Richard Whiting has arrived with his own and his decaased brother's family, making a party of eleven.
Edward Osborne and family are on the way, making as many more. Their tale is one of hardship and loss. Asked what they intended doing and whether they contemplated returning to Anticosti, Whiting said he intended settling down in Quebec city, where his family might enjoy the privileges of civilization, and that if he and his two brothers could get a little help, be would purchase a second-hand schooner with

which they would go below and engage in Ashing in the waters with which they were acquainted.
That is the treatment given to loyal Canadian citizens. 1 say that the treatment of these Fox Bay settlers from the Island of Anticosti forms a black period in the history of Canada. They were deprived of their homes to which by all the usages of this country they were fairly entitled. There is no part of Canada where the settler, who performs his duties as those Fox Bay settlers did for twenty-eight or thirty years, is refused permission to retain the land on which he has squatted or settled. They were fishermen, and farmers in a small way, and God-fearing, orderly citizens. They were driven out of their homes and transported-what do I hear ? The hon. member for Bellechase (Mr. Talbot) had better be careful of himself; we know his history pretty well.
Why do you not tell it if you know it ?
I have no hesitation in telling it.
Speak it out.
Order.
Make him keep order. I am speaking to the question and giving my opinions, and I hear various Improper and ill-bred interruptions from that quarter.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I have not made a single remark on anything he has said. I was speaking to a gentleman here.
I heard some improper remarks from where the hon. gentleman sits, anyway.
I do not care what you heard.

I was saying that these Fox Bay settlers were a desirable class of people to have retained in the Dominion of Canada. If they were driven from their homes by any process of law, it was a process of law which worked untold hardships on those men. After the season was over, and when it was impossible for them to cultivate the ground and earn their living, they were taken and placed in a district which was unfit for them to live in under any circumstances, and especially at a time of the year when it was impossible for them to make a living. Those men, women and children should have been the wards of the government, and those caresses and that assistance given to undesirable people should have been reserved for deserving Canadians like the Fox Bay settlers.
This government has an army of immigration agents in the old country. They have Mr. Devlin, formerly a member of this House, as immigration agent in the city of Dublin, and according to the statement of
my hon. friend from Lennox he has not had very great success. Out of 45,000 emigrants who left Ireland during the past year, only 765 came to Canada, or one out of every sixty. I am sorry that Irishmen or Englishmen or any man in the British Islands, when he moves, should not come to the Dominion, because we can offer him inducements not exceeded by any other country in the world. We can offer him the freest institutions, the greatest liberty, and that variety of occupation without which no country ever became great and prosperous.
We have Mr. Preston as a kind of roving commissioner with authority over all the other agents. Is he placed over Lord Strath-cona, and does he instruct that illustrious gentleman how he should conduct immigration matters in the city of London ? I presume he has the same authority over Lord Stratheona that he has over other immigration agents. We find that this roving agent has struck some new class of the population in Asia, and would like to have the fullest information from the hon. minister as to whether the government intend promoting the immigration of this class into Canada and can certify that they are a desirable class. I do hope the hon. gentleman will take warning by the mistakes his department has made in the past and try to bring out a desirable class of people-men from the northern parts of Europe, men from Great Britain, who are proved colonizers and settlers, and men like the Germans who assimilate with our people and become Canadian citizens, and are as proud of their country of adoption as of the country they left behind them. We do not want numbers regardless of any other consideration, which has been the text of the hon. member for Guysborough and other gentlemen, because population is not the great desideratum after all. If it were, China would be the greatest country in the world. What we want is the right stamp of men to lay the foundations of liberty and freedom in this country. We want those qualities which have made Canadians not inferior, but, I believe, superior to the people to be found anywhere else on the globe, and do not want those qualities to become degenerated by the importation of improper foreigners.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR Hon. Clifford Sifton). I have had occasion in this House to discuss that phase of the immigration question which has been discussed at such great length this afternoon and evening, and I should hardly deem it necessary to place again upon the records of the House the views I have already expressed at some length on a former occasion, not entertaining the same desire to repeat the same sentiments and opinions a number of times as some of my hon. friends opposite seem to have.
I have had during the past few years the pleasure of listening to the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (ivlr. Wallace)

upon a variety of occasions and subjects, and I have never heard him make a speech in this .House which was a fair presentation of the case, even from his own standpoint. I have never heard him resume his seat without appealing to the prejudices of some class of the community, and he has mis evening well sustained the reputation he has achieved of never neglecting an opportunity to strengthen himself politically by appealing to those prejudices which every states man ought to endeavour to allay. This evening he followed his usual tactics by dragging in by the heels a reference to the case of the Fox Bay settlers, which has no relevancy whatever to the subject we are discussing. That is purely a domestic matter not connected at all with the immigration policy of this department, one which ought to be discussed fairly, in the light of all the facts, properly stated, in order that the people may have a fair and proper conception of what has been done so as to decide whether or not the government is blamable.
But that is not my hon. friend's metnod of discussion. His method is to seize upon some ex-parte statement and proceed to dis cuss it. He does not even take the responsibility himself, but reads from a newspaper, in order that an unfair and dishonest statement of the facts may go before the people. In the experience I have had in connection .with the administration of thie affairs of this country, I do not know of any body of people who, having no claims on the government more than any other citizens of the country, have received such liberal, such considerate, -such judicious treatment as those to whom my hon. friend referred. If they have not been successful, I regret it.
Would the hon. minister tell us at what time of the year they were sent up to the North-west 1
I do not remember the exact time.
If I may be allowed a word-it was in the month of July or August.

There has never been a small body of people-or a large body for that matter-who have gone as new settlers to Manitoba or the North-west Territories, who have received the same kind and constant attention at the hands of this government and the officers of this government, as those to whom the hon. gentleman has referred. I need not say anything more about that. It has nothing to do with the discussion in hand, but was dragged in by the hon. gentleman in pursuance of his ordinary policy- for I am within the judgment of the House when I say that that hon. gentleman never rises without appealing to the prejudices of the people. My hon. friend has not thought fit to be extremely careful in the statements he has made. One hon. gentleman Mr. SIFTON.
on this side of the House said something about the Mennonites. There was no necessity for the hon. member for West York to travel outside the record to discuss the question of who brought the Mennonites into this country. He made the statement that it was the Conservative government which brought them in and the Liberals who opposed, as being the immigration of an undesirable people. The hon. gentleman's knowledge in this respect is greatly at fault. If he will look at the records of the House, he will find that the late Hon, Alexander Mackenzie was the man who made the loan and sent the Mennonites to the North-west amidst the denunciation of the political friends of the hon. gentleman-denunciations against his political character such as are addressed against us at this moment in reference to the Doukhobors.

I repeat the statement I made-I did not refer to the loan of the money-that the bringing in of the Mennon-ite settlers was arranged by the government of Sir John Macdonald, before they went out of office.

The Mennonites were sent to Manitoba as part of a policy which involved a loan which was arranged by the government of the late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. At page 379 of ' Hansard,' of 1875, the hon, gentleman will find the resolution with regard to this money.
They were in the country long before that, and the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) cannot deny it.

This policy of settling these people there was met with abuse of the Hon. Mr. Mackenzie for bringing them in, precisely as we are being abused now for bringing in the Doukhobors. We have been carrying out a policy of immigration which to-night for the first time has been denounced by a man sitting on the front bench of the Conservative party. For, as my hon friend from Selkirk well said, Sir Charles Tupper, when leader of his party, carefully refrained in any discussion that took place in this House, from expressing himself in any such terms as those that have been used by the hon. gentleman opposite in this debate. And, as I have shown, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) has spoken in total ignorance of the record of his own party on that question. Then, the hon. gentleman did not like the reference that was made by my hon. friend from Selkirk on the subject of the success attending the operations, in the York ton district, of the York Farmers' Colonization Company with which he is connected. I have sometimes been surprised at the statements made by the hon. gentleman in this House, but never so much so as at the remarks he has made in regard to that particular locality. One

*would have thought from the hon. gentleman's remarks that the York Farmers' Colonization Company had peopled that country *with those of British lineage and that the miserable Doukhobors and Galicians of that locality were a detriment, and prevented him from getting settlers for his lands. I can tell the hon. gentleman that the year before the Galicians went there, I drove over the York Farmers' Colonization tract, and I saw the abandoned mill, the stones of which had been taken out, and the walls of which stood tenantless, while the thousands of acres of the tract were unoccupied, the hon. gentleman not being able to dispose of the land or to get settlers for it. This will give an idea of the correctness of the information the hon. gentleman has given, this House. If he knew the facts, apparently he took pains to forget them before rising to speak. But I call attention also to the spirit of the hon. gentleman's remark. There seemed to be, on his part, a desire to leave a certain impression upon the House, an impression which certainly was not justified by the facts. What justification could the hon. gentleman have for speaking of the record of the Doukhobors and Galicians and saying that they might be murderers or anything else, that we might have had to hang a couple of them, but that the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) did not care so long as they were good servants in his house ? For what purpose was this ? The hon, gentleman sought to leave upon the public mind the impression that these people were of criminal tendency, that they were not of good character morally. I make the statement here that there is not an equal number of people in the Dominion of Canada among whom, for an equal length of time, there has been a lower record of crime than among these people. There is my challenge ; let the hon. gentleman take it up. He has no right to stand up, in this House, and seek to give the people of this country the impression that any class of people in Canada are of criminal tendency or have a criminal record when such is not the case. He said that it had been necessary to hang one of the Galicians. Well, it has been necessary to hang Canadians before this. But I say that the record of these people in connection with crime is not less favourable than that of the best class nationally speaking that can be found in Canada. 1 was struck with the wisdom of one remark made by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson). He said that as he did not know anything about the Doukhobors he would not express any opinion. If one or two other gentlemen would entertain and act upon the same sentiment, I think a good deal of the time of the House would be saved which has now been wasted.
I quite admit the right of the member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) to have an unfavourable opinion of the Galician people. It does not disturb me much that he has that feeling and expresses himself in an adverse way whenever discussions arises upon the subject in this House. The hon. member for Alberta and I have been friends for a good many years, I have known him for a long time, but I have never heard him express unqualified admiration for anything or any individual. There seems to be something about my hon. friend's constitution which, while it does not affect the keenness of his intellect, prevents him from expressing a favourable opinion about either men or things. Possibly it is a good thing for us to have one or two gentlemen of that class in the House, it keeps us from having too high an opinion of ourselves, and possibly there may be a corrective influence in his criticisms which have a beneficial effect upon us.
I will say one or two words about the general effect of the immigration policy of the government. One would think from the statements which have been made-and I think in that respect the member for Alberta was unfair to the member for Selkirk -one would think that the whole question of immigration as we have dealt with it in the last four years was a question of Doukhobors and Galicians. My hon. friend from Alberta said that the impression left upon his mind by the remarks of my hon. friend from Selkirk was that the prosperity of the North-west in the last few years was due to the influx of Doukhobors and Galicians. Well, I think if the member for Alberta will reflect for a few moments he will not consider that as a fair criticism of the remarks made by the hon. member for Selkirk. The member for Selkirk addressed almost all his remarks, and naturally so, to the criticisms which had been made upon the policy of the government and with the execution of which he had had a great deal to do himself. But my hon. friend from Selkirk knows well, knows better than any other member of this House, the exact proportion of people that have been brought into the North-west through the efforts of this government, and he knows that the Doukhobors and Galicians are comparatively a small proportion of the people that have been brought in there. This talk about the Doukhobors and Galicians has arisen almost entirely from the fact that our friends on the other side, having had for some years past the painful experience of failure in their immigration policy, think there is an opportunity of raising national prejudice against the policy of this government by attacking us upon that question. Forgetful of the record of their own party, careless of consistency so far as that is concerned, they endeavour to attack us particularly upon these two points, and they have endeavoured to lead the public mind to the supposition that we were bringing only these two classes into the country. The very first year after our taking office, something like 700 or 800 people came from the United States into

Manitoba and the North-west Territories; last year, Mr. Speaker, as a result of the organization which we have perfected in the western states, we brought no less than 15,000 settlers from the United States into Manitoba and the North-west Territories. This year our friends from the North-west who are familiar with what is going on at the present time, tell me, and the officers of my department tell me, there will be a considerably larger number. Sir, if the whole of the nearly half million dollars which we have expended had no other result in those three years than to bring those 20,000 people from the western states into this country, it would be one of the best expenditures the Dominion of Canada ever made.
Hon. gentlemen, I presume, were not serious when they said :	We will wait,
wait, we won't develop the country by bringing in population, but we will wait until the sons and daughters of Canadians spread themselves over the western prairies and become tillers of the soil. My hon. friends do not take the trouble to think what they are talking about. We get a few people in the shape of farmers from the older provinces, but don't my hon. friends know that the average young Canadian to-day does not want to go out on a western farm and grub there as his forefathers grubbed in the wilderness of eastern Canada ? The great majority of these young men desire a different kind of life, and they won't go there, and if you get them to go in the first place you cannot get them to stay. That has been to a large extent the experience that we have had in that western country. But, Mr. Speaker, what we should be able to do as a result of populating that country is this, we should be able to furnish those young men with profitable occupations of all kinds in the cities and towns of the west which will be built up upon the prairies, and in the cities and towns of British Columbia where mining and manufacturing interests are developing, where towns are going up upon the prairies about the Saskatchewan. We should be able in those towns and villages to furnish young Canadians occupations of a profitable character and of a class which they will be ready and willing to carry on. That will he the result. When you look over the scope of the development of our western country you will find that within the last three or four years young people from the province of Ontario have not been going to the western states as they did in former years. My hon. friend says we want people from the province of Ontario to go out on to these prairies. Why in the name of common sense did they not get people from the province of Ontario to go out on to those western prairies when they were in power ? But not at all. they went to the United States, and it was not until the last two or three years that the movement was entirely stopped, and those Mr. SIPTON.
young men are now going to Manitoba and the North-west Territories. That is the position, and as a result, thousands and thousands of young men can find a profitable occupation of a professional character, and clerical work of various kinds, all over that vast country.
Sir, I do not propose to discuss the question at greater length. I have only spoken as I did because I was impressed with the idea that the criticism of the hon. gentleman was most unfair and inaccurate, and his remarks were of such a character as to cast an aspersion upon people who had no right to be treated in that way. As I have said in this House before, I have not apologized. The hon. gentleman was not more accurate then than In the other statements he made. I did not apologize for anything the Department of the Interior done in regard to the policy of immigration. The hon. gentleman's statement in that respect was wholly inaccurate. I did not apologize, but I explained frankly to the House what had been done. I do not come before this House at any time for the purpose of saying that everything my department has done is entirely right, that everything my officers have done is absolutely and entirely right. I have spoken fully and frankly, as I always endeavour to do, of the operations of the department in respect to this work of immigration, and explained to t lie House in respect of the Galicians that though we were quite satisfied we could take care of a certain number of those people, we did not want unduly to increase the number, and we have made certain arrangements for the purpose of curtailing the movement and prevent it from unduly increasing. That is what I said, I did not in any way apologize, but I made a correct statement of what we have done. For my part, Mr. Speaker, so far as this particular class of people is concerned, the small proportion of them that have been taken into the North-west the last four years, I am satisfied that they are a very desirable people, and will make good citizens indeed, I have not the slightest doubt in the world about that. I fully agree with the statements which have been made by the member for Selkirk and the member for Saskatchewan in that respect.

I would like to say a word or two, not for the purpose of detaining the House at any length, but in justice to my hon. friend beside me (Mr. Wallace). The Minister of the Interior has confined his remarks to setting forth the great value of the Immigration policy pursued by him as compared with that of his predecessors, and with endeavouring to. cast some fine scorn upon the member for West York. But he did not answer anything that my hon. friend from West York said. He has told us that the Galicians are guilty of less crime than any other com-

munity in Canada. I do not know whether that is the case or not, hut it is no answer to what the member for West York said. It may be that what the Minister of the Interior said is absolutely correct; but 1 would point out to the hon. Minister of the Interior that when he makes that statement to the House it would be far better for him to give us some statistics so that we might judge as to the truth of his statement. Is he prepared to give us any statistics to bear out what he says ? I will sit down and let him do so if he can give us any. Well then, if he is not capable of giving us these statistics, why does he state to the House a fact of which he can have no knowledge whatever ? His ipse dixit is not to be the guide of the House unless he is able to support it by some facts. He also sneered at the hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) because that gentleman read a statement from the public press and did not make it on his own responsibility. I should think that the hon. Minister of the Interior is the last person in this House to throw such a sneer at an hon. member across the floor of the House, because, when charges were made in this House which would result in either driving him from public life, or the hon. member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) from public life, his followers voted down the motion for investigation which was asked for.
Now, so far as these Doukhobors and Galicians are concerned, I am ready to welcome them to Canada in such numbers as it is likely Canada is able to assimilate, provided they are not coming here with manners and customs which are likely to do injury to the general community in this country. I do not know what the marriage customs of the Doukhobors are, but I took notice that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), when he was dealing with this question, touched it very lightly. I would like an answer from that hon. gentleman merely for information, because I have no information on that subject myself, beyond what I see in the public press, and have heard in this House. The hon. gentleman seems to be familiar with the facts. Will he state yes or no as to the alleged custom of the Doukhobors putting away their wives without resort to any proceedings in court at all. It has been alleged in the public press, and I do not know whether it is correct or not, that this is a custom which prevails amongst them. I heard my hon. friend say that there has not been a divorce among them for a great many years, but that may be consistent with a custom such as has been referred to. I will give way to the hon. gentleman if he will make a statement on that point.

I thank my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) for the opportunity of probably making more plain anything 94	'
which I may have omitted to say this afternoon. I have read the book called The Christian Brotherhood, of which I have a copy in my desk, but that does not explain the marriage ceremony. I have also had many conversations with Doukhobors on this question. I have questioned them very closely about their belief in regard to the after life, and I was convinced from what I learned from them that their ideas were orthodox, that they were in accord with the general ideas held by Protestant people. In regard to their marriage ceremony, as far as ,1 could learn, when a young couple desire to marry the procedure is this : As you know they live in villages, and a great many live in the same house, the grandfather, the father and the grown-sons. There are probably twenty or thirty people living in one house. When a young couple desire to marry the question is studied very closely. Their temperament, their habits, the prospective husband's means of) supporting his wife are all considered. The fathers and grandfathers are required to take some time along with the young couple to consider whether or not the couple are suitable in temperament and habits. When it has been finally decided that they are suited for one another, they have a celebration of their own, and all their friends from the village and the neighbouring villages assemble. One of their elders-they do not call them elders-but one of their leading men in the village is supposed to, and as a matter of fact, does perform a certain rite by which he marries the young man and woman. There is no great ceremony about it ; a few words are uttered by which they become married. There has never been known to be but one divorce during all the time that this marriage ceremony lias existed in Russia. In so far as I can learn these are about the facts. I questioned a great many people, amongst them young Tolstoi and Prince Hilkoff, and as far as I could learn that is the way the marriage ceremony is carried out. As far as leaving their wives is concerned, it is simply ridiculous. Such a thing could not exist for four years and not come under my notice or under the notice of the officials. Such a practice has not been noticed by me. In regard to the marriage ceremony, I think that all that is required is simply a change in the law by which they will be enabled to register their marriages in a little different manner from that in which the Mennon-ites do, and there will be no trouble whatever.

I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman say what he has said, and I do not believe, if the customs of the Doukhobors are such as he states, and are otherwise of the character which has been described in this House, that there can be any particular objection to their becoming citizens of this country provided

they can be properly assimilated. But, I do not understand liow it happens that such a letter could have been written! as seems to have been written by some one in England to one of the Doukhobors in Manitoba with respect to their marriage customs. I am taking the statement that such a letter was written from hon. gentlemen in this House, and from the public press, and if a letter of that kind was written it certainly points to a different conclusion from that which the hon. gentleman has stated. I would think that the right hon. 'Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), or the hon. Minister of the Interior, if the customs of these people are not perfectly plain in that respect, might very well satisfy the) people of the country by making some definite inquiry into the matter. Surely it is easy enough to find out what their belief is in regard to these matters, and I for one would say that if such a custom as that of divorcing a wife without resorting to the courts prevails, they are not a class of people whom it is desirable to bring into this country. I do not suggest that such is the case, and I know that the hon. member for Selkirk, who has more knowledge of this subject than any other hon. gentleman in this House, says the contrary. Still, I do not understand how it happens that such a letter could have been written.
Mr. MeGREARY. I never heard of this letter until I heard of it here to-day. Who wrote this letter, and to whom was it written ?

I know nothing more of it than that I saw it in the public press, and that I heard what was stated about it here to-day. I do not assert that such a letter was written, nor do I suppose that the hon. member for Selkirk can assert that it was not written. It is a matter that may be inquired into by the hon. Minister of the Interior. If any such letter was written, if any such beliefs are entertained, it would be better that it should be settled once and for all in this country so that public opinion should not be disturbed by these rumours. Public opinion would be quieted by a definite statement from the government or some commission, or officer appointed by the government for the purpose of inquiring into it.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) let me interject a remark which seems to be very important ? Is he aware that the Doukhobors were endorsed and recommended by the Quakers Association of England and of the United States, and does; he not think that without knowing much of the religious ceremonies we may depend a great deal upon that endorsation ?
I am not saying a single word against the Doukhobors.

What I am suggesting is, that) when these rumours are in the public press, and when they are brought to the attention of the House, the government might very well make such inquiries as would place an authoritative statement before the people of Canada that no such practices had prevailed amongst these people. It is not desirable that public opinion should be influenced by rumours of that kind, which, according to the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. McCreary), are absolutely unfounded.

My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will understand that it was in that spirit I presented, as an offset against these rumours, the opinion of well known and most respectable organizations in the old country, in the United States and in Canada.	,

I am much obliged to my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) for the suggestion, and I think it affords additional reason why, if injustice is done to these people, they should be cleared in the minds of the population of this country from all such unjust aspersions. It is not conducive to the interests of Canada that these people should be living amongst us, and have their neighbours believe these things of them unjustly. I will not detain the House further with regard to that. I would suggest to the Minister of the Interior that we would like to have an explanation from him, when his estimates come on, as to what he proposes to do with respect to the expenditure for the purpose of inducing immigration from Ireland. The hon. gentleman did not touch at all what seemed to me to be the rather strong case put forward by my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) -namely, that although this government has spent a very large sum of money in Ireland, and should have secured a fair share of the emigration from that country, yet we got only 765 people out of the 45,000 who emigrated from Ireland last year. I need not say that the Irish people are a very desirable class of immigrants for Canada. They form a very large and respectable and important element in my own constituency, and I venture to think that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sifton) cannot expend money to better advantage than in inducing immigration from Ireland to Canada. I may say in passing, that I think, upon the whole, that it might be as well, so far as possible, to direct the best energies of the government to immigration from those countries from which the population of Canada has already been recruited. I refer to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and France, as well as Scandinavia and Germany, countries which possess people of practically the same stock as those of the British Isles. I believe that if we can supply the needs of this country, so far as population is concerned, from those

particular nations, it would be desirable to do so, and that the best efforts of the government should be directed to that end. It may not be a very desirable thing in the future that separate communities of Douk-hobors and Galicians, and various other nationalities from Russia and from Central Europe, should be growing up in the middle of the North-west. It may be desirable, to some extent, to have these people, but it is far more desirable to have immigrants from the British Isles, from France and Germany and Scandinavia. I will not detain the House further, but probably when the immigration estimates come up, I will have a word or two to say further.

I desire to call the attention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to the statement made by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), that the question of the observance of the marriage law by the Douk-hobor people was discussed by him, when immigration agent, with Mr. Haultain, the Attorney General of the North-west Territories, and that Mr. Haultain took the matter under advisement as to what course should be taken. The North-west Territories has a government of its own, and Mr. Haultain is a gentleman who is fully competent to deal with the matter. I think it would be very much better left under his charge than it would be in the Department of the Interior.

At this hour of the morning, I presume the House is not inclined to go into Committee of Supply, and I rise for the purpose of asking leave to withdraw the motion. Before I do so-and if it were not so late I would do it at a greater length-I wish to point out to my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Wallace) that he brought the Fox Bay settlers into this debate without any rhyme or reason, and he took occasion to make statements which were not warranted in fact, and which cannot be substantiated.
What was that ?

Everything that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) said. When he stated that these men ought to be the wards of the nation, I would like to know from him under what law can we make any citizen of Canada a ward of the nation ?
I said that while we were caressing the Doukhobors, surely we could have paid a little consideration to our own people, who were in distress.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) knows very well, that what he calls caressing the Doukhobors is done under the immigration law, and he also knows very well that there is no power
under the law to take people from one province into another province of the Dominion. He ought to know, if he does not know, that the Fox Bay settlers have been treated with the greatest consideration by this government ; without our being bound to do anything at all, but simply because of consideration for them. He ought to know, if he does not know, that if they were located on a swamp, as is stated in the paper which he quoted as his authority
I simply read the public press.

Yes, and what was his object in reading such statements, to which he will not give the sanction of his authority ? Is it not to raise prejudices in the minds of the community ? He is not prepared at this moment, even after he quoted the newspaper, to endorse it with his authority, but he was ready to incorporate it in his speech, so as to create the impression which I have spoken of. Let me say that if the Fox Bay settlers were settled in a swamp, they were not so settled by the Canadian government, because they were settled upon lands selected by their own friends, who fixed on the vicinity of a lake in order that these settlers, having been seafaring men all their lives, they could still engage in fishing operations. It is too late to discuss the subject at length now, but, I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) that if it pleases him at any other time, I shall be very glad to discuss this subject with him.

May I be permitted a word in reply. I read the article which appeared yesterday in the Ottawa Evening Journal, and I do not think that every article to which a member feels it his duty to call the attention of the government has to be certified as to its accuracy by the member reading it. The government know the facts. The government know whether these men have been placed in such a locality under such conditions and surroundings as has been stated in that paper. The government should know whether it is true that these men are returning, and that twelve of them died of disease out of a total number of-I cannot say how many, but I think sixty or seventy at the outside.
Sixty-one.

Twelve of them died out of a total of sixty-one. Are these statements true or are they not ti-ue ? The government should have information upon these facts, and I can tell the Prime Minister that when he characterized all my statements as untrue, I made no statement myself, except to say that the allegation appeared in a despatch from the city of Quebec to the Ottawa Evening Journal. I deemed it my duty to call the attention of the government

to this matter if they had not already known it, and I would have expected that a reply would have been given, and not the wholesale denial which the right hon. the Prime Minister has made. The statement of the Prime Minister does not deny that twelve of these people died of disease during the year they were up there.
That is not the fault of the government.

If these large lambs in the North-west are the result of the
government's paternal care, I suppose they ought to be able to exercise the same influence against disease amongst the Fox Bay settlers.

To find that twelve out of sixty-one of these settlers have lost their lives there, certainly does not recommend it as a healthy or proper place to send these poor people to.
Motion withdrawn.
